title: What Leaders Should Never Pay For
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article makes a pointed argument against a common leadership impulse: paying or formally incentivizing everyday collegial behavior like sharing ideas, giving feedback, or attending team events. The author contends that this destroys the intrinsic social contract of collaboration, converting colleagues into mercenaries who only help when compensated. Once that expectation takes hold, leaders are trapped, with no lever left except escalating payment. The piece closes by listing legitimate ways to build a collaborative culture — connection, empowerment, recognition, open communication — explicitly excluding pay as one of them.
points: Compensating people for ordinary collegial behavior — sharing ideas, giving feedback, attending team events — destroys the intrinsic motivation that sustains collaboration.
Once team members expect payment for collaborative acts, leaders lose any lever to encourage cooperation except more money, a trap that only escalates.
Formalized incentive systems intended to increase collaboration typically produce less of it over time as people go through the motions only when paid.
Sustainable collaboration should be built through connection, empowerment, recognition, and open communication — not extrinsic payment.
quotes: Chief among them is compensating people for being good citizens in the organization or team.
When leaders compensate people for being helpful and collaborative, they rob them of the intrinsic motivation to cooperate with their colleagues.
Leaders who mistakenly create formalized reward systems to promote collaboration actually get less of it over time.
Once team members believe they should be compensated for supporting and collaborating with others, leaders are stuck without any other appeal to action except more money.
Compensating for collaboration creates a sinkhole of expectation and destroys team morale over the long term.
